title: What Are Amazon Stock Bears Missing?
detail:
What Are Amazon Stock Bears Missing?
Trefis Team
Wed, September 23, 2026 at 10:55 AM MDT 4 min read
AMZN
MSFT
GOOG
META
WMT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

Amazon designs its own computer chips. That business may now be big enough to matter by itself. You probably picture Amazon as a giant store with a cloud arm. And you probably assume it buys its chips from someone else. Two things must be true for these chips to change how you see the stock. The first is size. The second is that owning the chips earns a return on the money Amazon is spending. Start with size.

How Big Is Amazon's Chip Business?

Management gave a number on its fiscal Q2 2026 call. The chips business runs at an annual revenue rate of over $25 billion. The business is growing at triple-digit percentages year over year. The chips sit inside AWS, the cloud unit. AWS revenue was $42.2 billion in that quarter. Revenue was up 36.7% from a year earlier. Annualized, AWS runs at $169 billion. So the chips are a real business. They are still only a slice of AWS, not the whole of it.

Amazon designs several custom chips. Its flagship processor for general-purpose computing is Graviton, which management said is used by 98% of the thousand largest customers of its EC2 compute service. The other is built for artificial intelligence work. Anthropic and OpenAI have made multi-year, multi-gigawatt commitments to that AI chip, management said. So size is settled. The second thing is harder.

Why Does That Matter While Amazon Spends So Heavily?

Because the spending is what worries people about this stock. Amazon expects to spend about $220 billion of cash on capital projects in 2026. Management blamed the higher cost of memory for the rise from its earlier plan of about $200 billion.

Against the index the picture is mixed. Amazon trades at 20.3 times its earnings. The S&P 500 trades at 22.6 times. On operating cash flow the order flips. Amazon trades at 17.0 times. The index trades at 14.7 times. Amazon's revenue has grown 13.0% a year over three years. By comparison, total aggregate S&P 500 revenue has grown at an annualized rate of 5.8% over the same period. The price appears to carry some doubt about what that spending will earn.

Owning the chips is management's answer. Management said the margins and returns in AI are tracking the core cloud business at the same stage. Management put them a little ahead. Management also said the order backlog stands at $496 billion. That backlog is growing triple digits year over year. And Amazon has more demand than it can serve in 2026. Management expects that again in 2027.

Owning the chips does not answer everything. Management did not put a profit figure on the chips. On returns you are taking management at its word. An analyst asked how a 39% cloud operating margin could be sustained. Management said margins will fluctuate with investment levels and mix. So what would tell you the second thing is failing?

title: Walmart has big plans for holiday bargain hunters
detail:
Walmart has big plans for holiday bargain hunters
Madison Troyer
Wed, September 23, 2026 at 9:33 AM MDT 4 min read
WMT
Trade Walmart on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

We may be only a few days into autumn, but Walmart, like many other retailers, already has its eyes on the holidays.

In a recent presentation at Goldman Sachs Global Consumer and Retail Conference, David Guggina, President and CEO of Walmart U.S., said the chain has already been working on its seasonal lineup.

Value-conscious shoppers, he noted, will be especially pleased with what's in store.

A new holiday lineup is taking shape at Walmart

When asked about Walmart's plans for the 2026 holiday season, Guggina said the retailer had been working on curating its seasonal assortment, with an emphasis on new products and sharp price points.

"We recently had our holiday meeting," he said. "The team is ready. We're ready to drive everyday low cost so that we can reinvest in the price and experience."

"Our merchants came with innovation. They came with new items, and they came with sharp price points," he continued. 

While Guggina didn't give particular details about the types of items and brand partnerships shoppers can expect to see in the coming months, he emphasized that the retailer intends to bring the same combination of assortment, value, and convenience that helped its back-to-school business.

"We're happy with how back-to-school has performed," he said. "We just had great assortment at great value and fantastic convenience, and that resonated with customers."

Looking to the next season, the Walmart U.S. CEO says shoppers should expect similar deals. 

"The consumer wants to save money and the consumer wants to save time, and we're going to allow them to do both of those things," he said.

Walmart is making value a bigger priority

Walmart's wallet-friendly holiday strategy isn't coming out of nowhere.

Earlier this year, the retailer pledged that it would be reinvesting a portion of its $2.9 billion tariff refund into price cuts and rollbacks on thousands of grocery and essential items.

"We took those [tariff] funds and we reinvested in price and experience," Guggina said at the September conference. "And with regards to price… there's really 2 ways that we utilize the funds. One is with rollbacks. So we had 11,200 rollbacks within the U.S. business. And another way is not taking price increases when we see the cost of goods come up, things like transportation and fuel costs, which have escalated."

This emphasis on value has helped Walmart maintain its position of preference with increasingly strained consumers.

"Right now, the U.S. consumer is resilient," Guggina said. "They're being very intentional with their dollars, and they're also looking for value. And that's why the Walmart value proposition is resonating today. We focus on low prices, and we focus on convenience."

The Zacks Retail – Supermarkets industry is benefiting from expanding omnichannel capabilities, rising digital engagement and growing demand for convenient shopping and meal solutions. Retailers are strengthening differentiation through private brands, prepared foods, loyalty programs and personalized offerings, while retail media and data-driven services are creating attractive new profit pools. At the same time, automation, artificial intelligence and better use of store networks should improve fulfillment efficiency and support digital profitability.

While labor, transportation, shrink and supply-chain costs continue to influence margins, retailers are pursuing productivity, sourcing and efficiency initiatives to manage these pressures. Against this backdrop, Walmart Inc. WMT, The Kroger Co. KR and Yesway, Inc. YSWY appear well positioned to capitalize on the industry's evolving growth opportunities.

About the Industry

The Zacks Retail – Supermarkets industry includes supermarket retailers that offer grocery, health and beauty aids, household chemicals, electronics, stationery, automotive accessories, hardware and paint, sporting goods, fabrics and crafts, entertainment products, home furnishings and more. Players in this industry operate through various formats such as supermarkets, multi-department stores, retail stores, discount stores, supercenters, hypermarkets and warehouse clubs. Food retail accounts for a chunk of their business. The industry has undergone a significant transformation over the years, with e-commerce playing a strong role. Given consumers' rising preference for online shopping, industry participants have enhanced pickup and delivery services and are offering easy payment options.

Major Trends Shaping the Future of the Supermarket Industry

Omnichannel Grocery Becomes a Stronger Growth Engine: Digital grocery is becoming an increasingly important part of the supermarket model as consumers seek greater convenience, faster delivery and seamless shopping across stores, apps and pickup channels. Retailers are using their physical store networks as fulfillment hubs while investing in automation, artificial intelligence and supply-chain technology to improve order accuracy and delivery economics. Demand is also shifting toward faster fulfillment, encouraging operators to expand same-day and rapid-delivery capabilities. Supermarkets with strong omnichannel platforms can increase shopping frequency, strengthen customer retention and capture a larger share of household spending.

title: Goldfish dives into protein with new cracker
detail:
Goldfish dives into protein with new cracker
Food Dive · Courtesy of The Campbell's Company
Christopher Doering
Wed, September 23, 2026 at 7:00 AM MDT 2 min read
WMT
Trade Walmart on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

This story was originally published on Food Dive. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily Food Dive newsletter.

Dive Brief:

Goldfish is diving into one of the biggest food trends with a protein-fortified version of the fish-shaped cracker, according to brand owner The Campbell's Company.

The new Goldfish has 6 grams of protein per serving and is available in cheddar and pizza flavors. The crackers will debut at Walmart and other grocery stores in October before expanding to retailers nationwide in early 2027. 

Protein continues to be in high demand among U.S. consumers, with 48% of adults saying they seek more of the nutrient in their diets, second only to vegetables, according to Circana's Eating Patterns in America report.

Dive Insight:

As demand for protein increases, food makers are seemingly including it in everything they can in order to boost sales and position products as healthier. PepsiCo's Doritos, Kraft Heinz's Mac & Cheese, J&J Snack Foods' Super Pretzels and Mars' Eggo waffles are just a few of the popular brands that have launched extensions with protein. Campbell's is just the latest company to enter the space.

"Protein has become a bigger priority for many families, whether it's after school, between activities or on the go," Tiphanie Maronta, senior vice president of Goldfish Crackers, said in a statement. "Goldfish made with 6g of Protein is our way of meeting that need with a snack that's both delicious and familiar."

After years of admitting it did not do enough to innovate the 64-year-old brand to keep it relevant, particularly among older consumers, Campbell's has been aggressively innovating the $1 billion Goldfish platform. Last month, Goldfish introduced the first gluten-free cheddar and reformulated whole grain versions of its smiling cheese crackers. 

Mick Beekhuizen, Campbell's CEO, noted in an earnings call earlier this month that Goldfish is seeing "encouraging progress" despite consumption declines in the company's salty snack business. Beekhuizen expressed confidence that efforts to position the brand as a family-friendly snack, in combination with the launch of a new marketing campaign, innovations and refreshed packaging, will benefit Goldfish over the long term.

title: Walmart Just Posted Its Lowest Operating Margin in Nine Years. Here’s What to Expect Next.
detail:
Walmart Just Posted Its Lowest Operating Margin in Nine Years. Here’s What to Expect Next.
Gian Estrada
Wed, September 23, 2026 at 5:09 AM MDT 4 min read
WMT
Trade Walmart on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Walmart Just Posted Its Lowest Operating Margin in Nine Years. Here's What to Expect Next. ©loonger and MiguelMalo from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Key Takeaways

Walmart's Q2 FY27 earnings call was framed around a 17.4% constant-currency jump in adjusted operating income, with CFO John David Rainey calling out incremental margins running twice the pace of the overall business.

TIKR's reported figures for the same quarter, ended July 31, 2026, show something else: operating income fell to $6.48 billion from $7.69 billion a year earlier, even as revenue rose to $187.94 billion from $177.40 billion.

Operating margin dropped to 3.45%, the lowest quarterly reading in the nine years, going back to fiscal 2017, below the 3.76% trough from early 2022 and every pre-pandemic print in between

Self-insurance costs, higher depreciation, the Vibe acquisition, and an opioid litigation settlement accrued the same quarter all landed on the GAAP line that the marketplace-and-advertising story is supposed to be lifting.

Walmart Stock's Second P&L Story Doesn't Show Up in Walmart's First One

On the Q2 2027 earnings call, John Furner and John David Rainey walked analysts through what has become Walmart's favorite phrase this year: the second P&L. Marketplace grew 52%. Advertising grew 38%, with Walmart Connect up 43%. Membership income rose nearly 17%.

A month later, at two separate investor conferences, Ryan Mayward and Manish Joneja got even more specific about the mechanics. Put a seller's inventory into Walmart Fulfillment Services and conversion jumps 50% at a cost 15% lower than the alternative. Layer advertising on top of that and GMV can jump five times over. Ad margins run above 70%, against roughly 5% for the core retail business. Rainey told analysts operating income grew 4x the rate of the U.S. comp, a level of profit growth the company said it hadn't produced in two decades.

None of that is fabricated. It is also, by the company's own admission, an adjusted, constant-currency figure that strips out a one-time benefit from $2.9 billion in tariff refunds Walmart received and mostly reinvested in price during the quarter.

WMT Stock Total Revenues and Operating Income (TIKR)
WMT Stock Operating Margins (TIKR)

Strip nothing out, and look at what actually printed on the income statement TIKR tracks: operating income for the July quarter came in at $6.48 billion, down from $7.69 billion the year before, a decline of roughly 16%, on revenue that grew nearly 6%.

Zoom out to the nine-year chart and the picture gets sharper. Outside the anomalous 2020-2022 stretch, when margin spiked as high as 6.24% on stimulus-fueled demand, Walmart's quarterly operating margin spent most of the prior decade oscillating between roughly 3.9% and 4.7%. The 3.45% posted this quarter sits below every one of those prints.
